about: The game scores behind the Brilliant library's famous-games shelf (batch 13, jobs/brilliancy-library-and-motif-coverage-2026-09-23, seeding source 3). `games`: each a famous game as a move list (or, with `fen`, a position and the moves from it), `who` as the card names it, and `why`: the explanation written for this app for each move that may enter the shelf, keyed by move as gates/make-brilliancy-classics.js names it (16.Qb8+, 17...Be6). A move enters chess.jsx's BRIL_CLASSICS only when it has a `why` here AND gates/fixtures/brilliancy-classics-measured.json records that the app's own engine and rule grade it Brilliant. Game scores are facts; no explanation is copied from anywhere. Every move list is replayed strictly (each move must be legal and written exactly as the app writes it) by the script and by gate 168. `threat`: for a move the game ENDED on (the opponent resigned), the line the move threatened, used as the card's line; it is analysis of a forced line, checked for legality by the tagger's own replay.

why.10.Nxb5: The knight takes a pawn the c-pawn guards. After cxb5, Bxb5+ pins the knight on d7 to the king, and Black never gets the pieces out.
why.13.Rxd7: The rook takes the pinned knight. After Rxd7 the other rook comes to d1, and the piece on d7 is pinned again and cannot be held.
why.16.Qb8+: The queen is given up to pull the knight off d7. After Nxb8 the d-file is open and Rd8 is mate.

why.5.Nxe5: The knight takes on e5 and leaves the queen to the bishop. If Bxd1, then Bxf7+ Ke7 and Nd5 is mate.

why.11.Rg1: The rook steps aside and leaves the bishop on b5 to the pawn. After cxb5, h4 and h5 chase the queen, and White gains the time to bring every piece out.
why.19.e5: A pawn move that leaves the second rook to be taken with check. It shuts the queen out of g7, and after Qxa1+ Ke2 White threatens Nxg7+ and mate.
why.22.Qf6+: The queen is given up to pull the knight off g8. After Nxf6 nothing guards e7, and Be7 is mate.

why.20.Rxe7+: The rook takes the knight with check. After Nxe7 the queen is given up on d7 as well, and the two bishops mate.
why.21.Qxd7+: The queen is given up to drag the king to d7. Bf5+ is then a double check, from the bishop and the rook on d1, and the bishops mate: Ke8, Bd7+ Kf8, Bxe7.

why.8.O-O-O: White castles and lets the knight on e4 be taken. After Nxe4 the queen is given up on d8, and it is mate in two more moves.
why.9.Qd8+: The queen is given up to drag the king onto the d-file. Bg5+ is then a double check, from the bishop and the rook, so the king must move, and it is mated on d8 either way.

why.17...Be6: The bishop comes to e6 and leaves the queen to be taken. After Bxb6 Bxc4+ the knight and bishop give check after check, win back far more than the queen cost, and the king never gets out.

why.23...Rd2: The rook lands on d2 where the queen can take it, to pull the queen away from the bishop on e4. After Qxd2 Bxe4+ Qg2 Rh3, mate on h2 cannot be stopped.

why.21.Ng5+: The knight leaves e6 with check, where the f-pawn can take it, and uncovers the queen's attack on d7. If fxg5, Qxd7 wins the queen.
why.22.Rxe7+: The rook takes the knight with check and cannot be taken: Qxe7 loses the rook on c8 with check, and Kxe7 runs into Re1+ and a mating attack. So the king steps aside and the rook follows it.
why.24.Rg7+: The rook still cannot be taken: Kxg7 loses the queen to Qxd7+ with check, and Qxg7 lets Rxc8+ in. The king is chased into the corner.

why.21.a4: A pawn is offered to pull the queen off b5. After Qxa4, Re4 hits it again, and it is running out of squares from which to guard e8.
why.22.Re4: The rook steps onto e4 where the queen could take it, but the queen must keep guarding e8. After Qb5, Qxb7 leaves it nowhere to go.

why.17.Bxg7: The second bishop goes too. After Kxg7, Qg4+ Kh7, Rf3 the rook swings to h3, and Black must give up the queen to stop mate.

why.9...Bxh2+: The bishop takes the h-pawn with check. If Kxh2, Ng4+ wins the knight on g5 back with an attack; after Kh1 the bishop stays to trouble the king.
why.13...Bg1: The bishop steps to g1, where it can be taken three ways, to clear h2 for the queen. After Nxg1 Qh2+ the king is driven into the open.
why.16...Ndxe5+: A knight is given up to open lines to the king: after fxe5, Nxe5+ brings the second knight in with check.
why.20...Bg4+: The bishop is given up to drag the king one square further. After Kxg4, Ne5+ is offered too, and h5 is mate.
why.21...Ne5+: The last knight is given up to take away the king's squares. After fxe5, the pawn move h5 is mate.

why.24.Rxd4: The rook is given up on d4 to open the way to the king. After cxd4, Re7+ comes, and the king is pulled up the board: Kb6, Qxd4+ Kxa5, b4+ Ka4.
why.25.Re7+: A second rook is offered with check. It cannot be taken: Qxe7 allows Qxd4+ and mate soon after. So the king walks forward, into the net.
why.26.Qxd4+: The queen takes on d4 with check and leaves the knight on a5 to the king. After Kxa5, b4+ Ka4 the king is cut off on the edge of the board.
why.37.Rd7: The rook is offered on d7 to pull the black rook off the d2 square. After Rxd7, Bxc4 wins the queen, because bxc4 then loses the rook on h8 to the queen.

why.30.Qh8+: The queen is given up to drag the king to h8. After Kxh8, Nxf7+ forks the king and the queen, and White comes out a knight ahead.
